title: Berkshire Earnings Beat Forecasts as Abel Accelerates Buybacks to $4.5 Billion
excerpt: Operating profit rose 16% to $12.98 billion in the conglomerate's second quarter under CEO Greg Abel, while share repurchases surged nearly 20-fold from Q1.
body:
• Operating earnings rose 16% to $12.98 billion, topping analyst estimates of $10.58 billion, driven by strength at BNSF railroad and service businesses.
  • Berkshire repurchased $4.5 billion of stock in Q2, up from $235 million in Q1, with an additional $3.3 billion bought back in July.
  • The company's cash pile fell to $364.7 billion from a record $380.2 billion as Berkshire became a net buyer of stocks for the first time in 14 quarters.
  • Geico's pre-tax underwriting profit plunged 45%, with an analyst calling the results "absolutely abysmal" amid rising claims and marketing costs.

Berkshire Hathaway reported second-quarter operating earnings of $12.98 billion on Saturday, a 16% increase from a year earlier that comfortably beat Wall Street expectations, as CEO Greg Abel's first full year at the helm showed accelerating capital deployment and the largest share repurchase program in years.

Net income more than doubled to $25.67 billion, or about $17,868 per Class A share, bolstered by $12.68 billion in investment gains. Revenue rose 10% to $101.81 billion. Berkshire has urged investors to focus on operating results rather than net income, which includes unrealized gains and losses on stocks the company still holds.

Abel Unleashes the Buyback Machine

The standout figure in the quarterly report was the dramatic acceleration in stock repurchases. Berkshire bought back $4.5 billion of its own shares between April and June — a nearly 20-fold increase from the $235 million it spent in the first quarter, when Abel had just resumed buybacks after a nearly two-year hiatus.

The buying didn't stop at quarter's end. Through July 29, Berkshire repurchased an additional $3.3 billion of stock, according to the company's 10-Q filing, putting the conglomerate on pace for its most aggressive buyback year since 2021, when it retired $27 billion in shares.

The bulk of Q2 purchases came in June. Berkshire paid a weighted average of $731,389 per Class A share and $485.95 per Class B share — both well below Friday's closing prices of $780,086 and $521.80, respectively, suggesting Abel and Buffett saw meaningful value.

"It's a pretty healthy beat, and investors will be encouraged. Slowly, gradually and subtly we're seeing Greg assert himself as the new leader."

— Cathy Seifert, analyst at CFRA Research

Cash Pile Shrinks for First Time in Four Years

Berkshire ended June with $364.7 billion in cash and Treasury bills, down from a record $380.2 billion three months earlier. It marked the first sequential decline in the company's cash position in four years.

Beyond buybacks, Berkshire bought nearly $20 billion more stocks than it sold during the quarter, ending 14 consecutive quarters as a net seller of equities. Among the purchases: a $10 billion addition to its already-large position in Alphabet, the parent of Google and YouTube, which is now one of Berkshire's largest holdings.

The company also closed on the $6.8 billion acquisition of home builder Taylor Morrison in late July, signaling Abel's willingness to pursue large deals that had become rare under Buffett in recent years.

"It's very hard to want Greg to be making big deals in an ebullient market like now. The private markets are insane, and the public markets are kind of silly, too."

— Paul Lountzis, president of Lountzis Asset Management

Geico Stumbles While Railroads and Energy Gain

The results weren't uniformly positive. Geico, Berkshire's auto insurance unit, saw pre-tax underwriting profit fall 45% as accident claims rose and the company ramped up marketing spending to regain customers lost during a multi-year effort to improve underwriting quality.

Seifert called Geico's results "absolutely abysmal" and flagged "red flags" at a time rivals including Allstate and Progressive are posting stronger numbers. Overall insurance and reinsurance profit fell 11%.

The weakness was more than offset by gains elsewhere. BNSF railroad profit rose 6% to $1.56 billion on higher volumes of consumer, agricultural, and energy products. Berkshire Hathaway Energy posted a 27% profit increase to $891 million, benefiting from higher utility margins and tax credits. Service businesses including NetJets and TTI electronic components also contributed to the beat.

What to Watch

Berkshire flagged "considerable uncertainty" around macroeconomic and geopolitical events, including tariffs and trade wars, noting shifting demand at consumer-facing businesses like Fruit of the Loom and Forest River recreational vehicles.

The quarter was Abel's second as CEO. Buffett, who turns 96 on August 30, remains chairman and told CNBC last month that he's still involved in decision-making, with neither he nor Abel acting without the other's approval.

Berkshire's Class A shares are up 3% in 2026, trailing the S&P 500's 13% gain. Investors will get more detail on the company's equity purchases when it files its 13-F with the SEC around August 14.
